title: The Racing Line
intro: The racing line is the path round a track that gives the lowest lap time. It is not the shortest path. It is the path that makes each corner as wide and gentle as possible, so the car can carry more speed, and that gets the car onto the following straight as fast as possible. This page covers the parts of a corner, how to choose an apex, how to handle different kinds of corner and sequences of corners, and the reference points drivers use to drive the line the same way every lap.

items: Braking point: where the driver starts braking, usually on the straight before the corner and in a straight line.
Turn-in point: where the driver starts steering. On the classic line it is at the outside edge of the track.
Apex (clipping point): the point where the car comes closest to the inside of the corner, usually touching the inside kerb.
Exit (track-out point): where the car reaches the outside edge again as the steering unwinds and the throttle goes on.
Entry, mid-corner and exit phases: drivers describe handling problems by phase ("understeer on entry", "loose on exit"), and setup changes act on each phase differently.

blocks.text: The basic line for a single corner starts at the outside edge, cuts to the inside at the apex and runs back out to the outside edge. Using the full width of the track this way gives the largest possible radius, and since the fastest cornering speed grows with the square root of the radius (see #/racing/vehicle-dynamics), a wider arc is a faster one. The line with one constant radius that just touches the outside, the inside, and the outside again is called the geometric line. It gives the highest minimum speed through the corner.
Late apex: trading corner speed for exit speed

The geometric line is rarely the fastest. What matters is the time over the whole lap, and the speed a car carries out of a corner is carried all the way down the following straight. A late apex line turns in later, makes a tighter turn early in the corner, touches the inside further round, and then has a straighter, wider exit. The car is slower at the apex, but it can begin accelerating earlier and harder because it needs less steering on exit. On a corner leading onto a long straight this gain is worth much more than the loss in the corner. Turning in later also means braking later, in a straight line, which is where the car brakes best.

blocks.alt: A 90-degree right-hand corner seen from above. A blue line runs from the outside of the approach straight in one wide constant-radius arc to the inside and out to the far edge. A red late-apex line stays straight longer, turns more sharply, touches the inside kerb further round and runs out onto the exit straight in a gentle curve.
blocks.caption: The geometric line (blue) is a single arc; the late-apex line (red) brakes later, turns tighter at first, and straightens the exit so the throttle can go on sooner.

blocks.text: An early apex (turning in too soon and touching the inside before the geometric apex) is the most common mistake. The car arrives at the inside too early, still has a lot of corner left to turn, and runs out of track on exit: the driver has to lift off or run wide. When in doubt, apex later.
Corners are not equally important. A useful ranking, from Carroll Smith and many driving coaches:

items: Most important: a corner leading onto a long straight. Sacrifice entry speed for the best possible exit speed (late apex).
Next: a corner at the end of a long straight. Here the time is in the braking zone: brake as late as possible and accept a compromised exit, because a short straight follows.
Least important: a corner between two other corners. Use whatever line sets up the next, more important corner.
Hairpin: a slow turn of about 180 degrees. Brake late and deep, rotate the car near the middle, and focus entirely on the exit.

Fast sweeper: a long, fast bend. Small changes of speed cost a lot of time; the line is close to geometric, and smooth, minimal steering corrections keep the tyres near their peak. Downforce matters most here.
Decreasing-radius corner: one that tightens as it goes. The apex comes later than it looks; turn in late and be patient.
Increasing-radius corner: one that opens out. The car can accelerate early; an earlier apex often works.
Chicane: two or more quick corners in opposite directions. Straighten it as much as possible by using the kerbs, and sacrifice the first part to exit the last part well.
Esses and complexes: a series of linked corners. Treat them as one problem and work backwards from the exit of the last one.
Crests, dips and camber: a corner that falls away (off-camber) or crests a hill has less grip, because the tyres are pressed down less; a banked corner or a dip (compression) has more.

blocks.text: Drivers drive the same line every lap by picking reference points: a braking board, a crack in the tarmac, a kerb stripe, a tyre mark, a tree on the horizon. A good driver uses several per corner (where to brake, where to turn in, where the apex is, where the car will track out) and looks ahead to the next one before reaching the current one. In a simulator the same habit works; games that draw a racing line or braking markers on the track are a crutch to learn from and then switch off, because they do not adapt to the car, the tyres or the traffic.

Most series define the track as the area inside the white lines, with the kerbs included; a car is usually allowed to have two wheels outside. Using the run-off to gain time is penalised, by deleting the lap time in qualifying or by penalties in a race. Many racing games enforce limits the same way, with warnings and time penalties.
When to drive off the classic line

items: In the wet: the classic line is polished and coated with rubber and oil, so in the rain it is often the slipperiest part of the track. Drivers move off it to find grip on the cleaner surface.
When defending or attacking: an overtaking move often requires a tighter, compromised line (see #/racing/racecraft).

Different cars want different lines: a high-power car gains most from a late apex and a straight exit; a low-power car or a kart, which cannot regain lost speed, wants to keep its momentum and uses a more rounded line.
Tyre saving: taking a little less kerb and a smoother line reduces wear in long races.

blocks.title: Which corner matters most?
blocks.text: A lap has a slow hairpin leading onto a 1 km straight and a fast kink leading onto a 100 m straight. Where should a driver accept losing time to gain it elsewhere?
blocks.hint: Speed at the exit of a corner is carried down the whole of the straight after it.
solution: Take the hairpin with a late apex and give up some speed in the corner for the best possible exit. Every 1 km/h gained at the exit is carried for the whole kilometre.
At the kink, the short straight after it means exit speed counts for little; the line that keeps the most speed through the kink itself is best.

blocks.text: Sources: Smith, C. (1996), Drive to Win, Carroll Smith Consulting, chapters on the line and corner priority. Bentley, R. (1998), Speed Secrets, Motorbooks. Taruffi, P. (1959), The Technique of Motor Racing, G. T. Foulis. Lopez, C. (2001), Going Faster! Mastering the Art of Race Driving, Bentley Publishers.
